workEn: The Four Branches of the Mabinogi
title: Pwyll Pendeuic Dyuet
titleEn: Pwyll, Prince of Dyfed — The rider at the mound of Arberth
part: The rider at the mound of Arberth
source: Pedeir Keinc y Mabinogi, First Branch, from the White Book of Rhydderch (NLW Peniarth 4, c. 1350) as printed in J. Gwenogvryn Evans, The White Book Mabinogion (Pwllheli, 1907), columns 12–19; public domain. Readings are the manuscript's as Evans prints them, checked against the page images; word division, punctuation, capitals and quotation marks are ours. Where the White Book omits a word the sense requires, it is supplied from the Red Book (Rhŷs & Evans) and the note says so. Pronunciation convention: the manuscript spelling read with the sounds of Welsh c. 1300. Translations made fresh from the Welsh.

sentences.t: A threigylgueith yd oed yn Arberth, prif lys idaw, a gwled darparedic idaw, ac yniueroed mawr o wyr y gyt ac ef.
sentences.l: And one-time he-was in Arberth, chief court to-him, and a-feast prepared for-him, and great hosts of men together with him.
sentences.i: And once he was at Arberth, his chief court, and a feast had been prepared for him, and great companies of men were with him.
sentences.n: The same opening as the first part (threigylgueith, spelt here with gu for gw): A threigylgueith 'and once', t > th after a 'and'. yd oed 'he was', with yd because the sentence does not open with its subject. prif lys idaw 'a chief court to him' = his chief court; idaw 'to him' is a conjugated preposition (y/i 'to' + -aw). darparedic 'prepared' is a past participle in -edic (darparu 'prepare'). yniueroed is the plural of yniuer (= niuer) 'company, host'. o wyr 'of men' ← gwyr, soft-mutated after o. y gyt ac ef 'together with him'.

sentences.t: A guedy y bwyta kyntaf, kyuodi y orymdeith a oruc Pwyll, a chyrchu penn gorssed a oed uch llaw y llys, a elwit Gorssed Arberth.
sentences.l: And after the first eating, rising to walk-about he-did, Pwyll, and making-for the top of a-mound that was above the court, that was-called the Mound of-Arberth.
sentences.i: And after the first sitting at table, Pwyll rose to take a walk, and made for the top of a mound above the court, called the Mound of Arberth.
sentences.n: kyuodi … a oruc Pwyll 'rising Pwyll did' = Pwyll rose: the verbal noun first, then a oruc, and the subject after it. y bwyta kyntaf 'the first eating' is the first sitting of the feast. y orymdeith 'to walk about' ← gorymdeith, soft-mutated after y 'to'. a chyrchu 'and making for' ← kyrchu, spirant mutation after a 'and'. gorssed (modern gorsedd) is a mound, the kind a lord might sit on; uch llaw 'above'. a elwit 'that was called' is the impersonal imperfect in -it (galw 'call'), soft-mutated after a.

sentences.t: “Arglwyd,” heb un o'r llys, “kynnedyf yr orssed yw, pa dylyedauc bynnac a eistedo arnei, nat a odyno heb un o'r deupeth, a'y kymriw neu archolleu, neu ynteu a welei rywedawt.”
sentences.l: “Lord,” said one of the court, “the property of the mound it-is, whatever nobleman that may-sit on-it, that he-goes-not from-there without one of the two-things: either injury or wounds, or else he-would-see a-wonder.”
sentences.i: “Lord,” said one of the court, “it is the property of the mound that whatever man of rank sits on it does not leave it without one of two things: either hurts or wounds, or else he sees a wonder.”
sentences.n: kynnedyf 'peculiar property, nature'; the predicate comes first and yw 'is' follows. pa dylyedauc bynnac 'whatever nobleman': dylyedauc 'man of birth' (from dylyet 'right, due') has d as its own first letter, so pa, which softens, shows nothing here; bynnac 'ever'. a eistedo is the present subjunctive in -o, 'may sit'. arnei 'on it' (the mound is feminine). nat a odyno 'that he does not go from there': a is 'goes', the present of mynet. deupeth 'two things'. a'y kymriw: our text divides the word as a'y (the division and apostrophe are editorial), as if a 'with' + 'y 'his'; but 'with his injury' makes no sense after 'one of the two things', and 'his' would have softened the noun to gymriw. The unmutated kymriw and the neu 'or' that follows show the conjunction ae 'either' (ae … neu 'either … or'), and the Red Book has ae kymriw ae archolleu, 'either injury or wounds'. Read it as ae. kymriw 'injury, bruising' and archolleu 'wounds' are near-synonyms. rywedawt is the scribe's spelling of ryuedawt 'wonder' (w for u = v), spelt normally in the next sentence and in the Red Book. neu ynteu 'or else'; a welei 'would see', with the verbal particle a, is an imperfect and sits oddly after the present tenses.

sentences.t: “Nyt oes arnaf i ouyn cael kymriw neu archolleu ym plith hynn o niuer. Ryuedawt hagen da oed gennyf pei ys guelwn. Mi a af,” heb ynteu, “y'r orssed y eisted.”
sentences.l: “There-is-not on-me fear of-getting injury or wounds among this-much of company. A-wonder, however, good it-would-be with-me if I-saw-it. I it-is-that will-go,” said he-for-his-part, “to the mound to sit.”
sentences.i: “I have no fear of getting hurts or wounds among such a company as this. A wonder, though, I should be glad to see. I will go,” he said, “to the mound and sit.”
sentences.n: Nyt oes arnaf i ouyn 'there is no fear on me': fear, like colour, is 'on' a person; arnaf is ar 'on' + -af 'me'. ouyn is ofn 'fear', u = v. hynn o niuer 'this (much) of company'. hagen 'however'. da oed gennyf 'it would be good with me' = I should like: gennyf 'with me' is gan conjugated. pei ys guelwn 'if I saw it': pei 'if' for what is not so, ys the infixed 'it', guelwn the imperfect subjunctive, first person (gwelet). Mi a af 'I will go': the abnormal sentence, subject then a then the verb, the present serving as future. heb ynteu 'said he for his part'. y'r = y 'to' + 'r 'the'.

sentences.t: Eisted a wnath ar yr orssed.
sentences.l: Sitting he-did on the mound.
sentences.i: He sat down on the mound.
sentences.n: Eisted a wnath: the verbal noun, then a and a form of gwneuthur 'do'. The manuscript has a wnath, a scribal slip for a wnaeth 'he did'; Evans prints it so and it is kept as written.

sentences.t: Ac wal y bydynt yn eisted, wynt a welynt gwreic ar uarch canwelw mawr aruchel, a gwisc eureit llathreit o bali amdanei, yn dyuot ar hyt y prifford a gerdei heb law yr orssed.
sentences.l: And as they-were sitting, they it-was-that saw a-woman on a-horse pale-white big very-tall, and a-garment golden shining of brocade about-her, coming along the highway that went past the mound.
sentences.i: And as they sat there, they saw a woman on a great, tall, pale-white horse, with a shining garment of gold brocade about her, coming along the high road that ran past the mound.
sentences.n: wal is ual 'as', written with the w-letter for the v-sound. y bydynt 'they were (being)': bydynt is the habitual imperfect of bot (beside oedynt), usual in 'as they were …' clauses. wynt a welynt 'they saw': the abnormal sentence again, with the imperfect plural. gwreic is the object, written unmutated (an object is often soft-mutated, wreic). ar uarch ← march, soft after ar 'on'. canwelw 'pale white' (can 'white' + gwelw 'pale'); aruchel 'very high' (ar- + uchel). eureit 'golden' (aur), llathreit 'shining'; o bali ← pali 'brocade, silk', soft after o. amdanei 'about her', am conjugated. a gerdei 'that went' ← kerdei, soft after a. heb law 'past, alongside'.

sentences.t: Kerdet araf guastat oed gan y march ar uryt y neb a'y guelei, ac yn dyuot y ogyuuch a'r orssed.
sentences.l: A-pace slow even was with the horse to the mind of anyone who saw-it, and coming to as-high-as the mound.
sentences.i: To anyone watching, the horse's pace was slow and even; and it was coming level with the mound.
sentences.n: Kerdet 'going, pace' is here a noun, put first as the predicate, with oed 'was' after it; gan y march 'with the horse' = the horse had. ar uryt ← bryt 'mind', soft after ar: 'in the mind of', to the eye of. y neb a'y guelei 'anyone who saw it/her': a relative + 'y infixed object. y ogyuuch a'r orssed 'to (as) high as the mound' = level with it: gogyuuch (modern gogyfuwch 'level with', go- + kyuuch, the equative of uchel 'high') is soft-mutated after y 'to' (the Red Book has yn ogyfuuch).

sentences.t: “A wyr,” heb y Pwyll, “a oes ohonawch i a adnappo y uarchoges?”
sentences.l: “O men,” said Pwyll, “is-there of-you who may-know the horsewoman?”
sentences.i: “Men,” said Pwyll, “is there any of you who knows the horsewoman?”
sentences.n: A wyr 'O men' — the vocative a with soft mutation (gwyr). heb y Pwyll 'said Pwyll', with y, the article, before the name, as in the first part. a oes 'is there?' — a is the question particle. ohonawch i 'of you' (o conjugated, plural); the i that Evans spaces off is probably the echoing pronoun chwi with its ch run into the ending. a adnappo 'who may know' is the present subjunctive of adnabot 'recognize'. y uarchoges ← marchoges 'horsewoman' (march + feminine -oges): the article softens a feminine noun.

sentences.t: “Nac oes, Arglwyd,” heb wynt.
sentences.l: “There-is-not, Lord,” said they.
sentences.i: “No, Lord,” they said.
sentences.n: Nac oes 'there is not': Welsh has no bare 'no', so the answer repeats the verb, with the answering negative nac. heb wynt 'said they'.

sentences.t: “Aet un,” heb ynteu, “yn y herbyn y wybot pwy yw.”
sentences.l: “Let-go one,” said he-for-his-part, “to-meet her to know who she-is.”
sentences.i: “Let one of you go to meet her,” he said, “and find out who she is.”
sentences.n: Aet 'let him go', the third-person imperative of mynet. yn y herbyn 'to meet her' (literally 'in her meeting'): y 'her' puts h- before a vowel (erbyn). y wybot 'to know' ← gwybot, soft after y 'to'. Two of the five jobs of y side by side: 'her' and 'to'; the others are 'his' (soft mutation), the article, and the verbal particle.

sentences.t: Un a gyuodes y uynyd, a phan doeth yn y herbyn y'r ford, neut athoed hi heibaw.
sentences.l: One it-was-that rose up, and when he-came to-meet her to the road, lo she-had-gone past.
sentences.i: One of them got up, and when he came out to the road to meet her, she had already gone by.
sentences.n: a gyuodes 'rose', the preterite in -es (kyuodi), soft after a. y uynyd 'up' ← mynyd 'mountain' (literally 'to the mountain'). ford is ffordd 'road', f for ff. neut is the affirmative particle neu 'lo, indeed' in the form it takes before a vowel (as yd beside y); it is not an infixed pronoun. athoed 'had gone', the pluperfect of mynet. heibaw 'past'.

sentences.t: Y hymlit a wnaeth ual y gallei gyntaf o pedestric.
sentences.l: Her pursuing he-did as he-could fastest on foot.
sentences.i: He ran after her as fast as he could on foot.
sentences.n: Y hymlit 'her pursuing': the object of a verbal noun is a possessive before it, and y 'her' prefixes h- (ymlit 'pursue'). ual y gallei gyntaf 'as he could fastest' — gyntaf ← kyntaf, the superlative of buan 'swift', softened. o pedestric 'on foot' (unmutated after o, as the scribe often leaves it): pedestric is a borrowing from Latin pedester 'on foot', but its exact meaning is disputed — 'going on foot' fits here, while below it is used of a horse, which points rather to 'speed, running'.

sentences.t: A fei mwyf uei y urys ef, pellaf uydei hitheu e wrthaw ef.
sentences.l: And the most would-be his haste, the farthest she-for-her-part would-be from-him.
sentences.i: And the greater his haste, the farther from him she was.
sentences.n: pei … pellaf 'the more … the farther': pei, here written fei (= phei, the spirant after a 'and'), works like modern po in 'the more … the more'. mwyf is a scribal slip for mwyaf 'most' (the Red Book has vwyhaf, softened), kept as Evans prints it. uei ← bei 'would be', the imperfect subjunctive of bot, soft-mutated. y urys ef 'his haste' ← brys, soft after y 'his'. uydei ← bydei 'would be'. hitheu 'she for her part'. e wrthaw ef 'from him' (y wrth 'away from', wrthaw conjugated).

sentences.t: A phan welas na thygyei idaw idaw y hymlit, ymchwelut a oruc at Pwyll a dywedut wrthaw.
sentences.l: And when he-saw that it-availed-not to-him to-him her pursuing, returning he-did to Pwyll and saying to-him.
sentences.i: And when he saw that it was no use to him to chase her, he went back to Pwyll and told him.
sentences.n: welas 'saw', the preterite in -as (gwelet). na thygyei 'that it did not avail' — na, the negative 'that not', with spirant mutation of tygyei, imperfect of tygyaw 'avail, profit'. idaw idaw: the scribe wrote 'to him' twice, a slip of repetition printed as written; read it once (the Red Book has it once). ymchwelut a oruc 'returning he did' = he went back; a dywedut 'and saying', the verbal noun carrying on.

sentences.t: “Arglwyd,” heb ef, “ni thykya y pedestric yn y byt e hymlit hi.”
sentences.l: “Lord,” said he, “avails-not the foot-speed in the world to-pursue her.”
sentences.i: “Lord,” he said, “no running in the world is any use for chasing her.”
sentences.n: ni thykya 'does not avail', present of tykyaw, spirant after ni. y pedestric yn y byt 'the running in the world' = any running: pedestric again (see above). e hymlit hi 'to pursue her' — e is y 'her' with h-, and hi doubles the pronoun.

sentences.t: “Ie,” heb ynteu Pwyll, “dos y'r llys, a chymer y march kyntaf a wypych, a dos ragot yn y hol.”
sentences.l: “Yes,” said he-for-his-part Pwyll, “go to the court, and take the first horse that you-may-know, and go before-you after her.”
sentences.i: “Yes,” said Pwyll, “go to the court, take the first horse you know of, and go on after her.”
sentences.n: heb ynteu Pwyll 'said he for his part, Pwyll'. dos 'go!', the imperative of mynet. a chymer 'and take' ← kymer, spirant after a. a wypych 'that you may know', the present subjunctive of gwybot. dos ragot 'go before you' = go on; ragot ← racot, rac 'before' conjugated, soft-mutated. yn y hol 'after her' (ol 'track', h- after y 'her').

sentences.t: Y march a gymerth, ac racdaw yd aeth.
sentences.l: The horse he-took, and before-him he-went.
sentences.i: He took the horse and went on his way.
sentences.n: Y march a gymerth: the object comes first, then a and the verb (kymerth, preterite of kymryt, soft after a). racdaw 'before him' (rac conjugated); yd aeth 'he went', with yd because something other than the subject opens the clause.

sentences.t: Y maestir guastat a gauas, ac ef a dangosses yr ysparduneu y'r march.
sentences.l: The open-land level he-got, and he it-was-that showed the spurs to the horse.
sentences.i: He reached the level open ground and showed the horse his spurs.
sentences.n: maestir 'open land' (maes 'field' + tir 'land'). a gauas 'got, reached', preterite of caffael, soft after a. a dangosses 'showed', preterite in -es (dangos). ysparduneu 'spurs', plural of yspardun.

sentences.t: A ffei uwyaf y lladei ef y march, pellaf uydei hitheu e wrthaw ef.
sentences.l: And the most he-would-strike the horse, the farthest she-for-her-part would-be from-him.
sentences.i: And the harder he drove the horse, the farther from him she was.
sentences.n: The same 'the more … the farther' pattern: ffei is phei (pei after a 'and'), now with uwyaf correctly spelt (mwyaf, soft-mutated). lladei is the imperfect of llad, which means 'strike' as well as 'kill'.

sentences.t: Yr vn gerdet a dechreuyssei hitheu yd oed arnaw.
sentences.l: The same pace that she-for-her-part had-begun, it-was on-it.
sentences.i: Her horse kept to the very pace she had begun with.
sentences.n: Yr vn gerdet 'the same pace' (vn = un 'one'; with the article, 'the same'; gerdet ← kerdet, soft after it). a dechreuyssei 'that she had begun' is the pluperfect in -yssei (dechreu). yd oed arnaw 'was on it' — on her horse.

sentences.t: Y uarch ef a ballwys; a phan wybu ef ar y uarch pallu y bedestric, ymchwelut yn yd oed Pwyll a wnaeth.
sentences.l: His horse it-was-that failed; and when he-knew from his horse its speed failing, returning to where was Pwyll he-did.
sentences.i: His horse gave out; and when he could tell from his horse that its speed was failing, he went back to where Pwyll was.
sentences.n: Y uarch ef 'his horse' ← march, soft after y 'his'. a ballwys 'failed', the preterite in -wys of pallu, soft after a. wybu 'knew', preterite of gwybot. pallu y bedestric 'its speed failing' ← pedestric, soft after y 'its' — said of a horse, which is why 'speed' seems the sense. yn yd oed 'where (he) was'.

sentences.t: “Arglwyd,” heb ef, “ny thykya y neb ymlit yr unbennes racco. Ny wydwn i warch gynt yn y kyuoyth no hwnnw, ac ni thygyei ymi y hymlit hi.”
sentences.l: “Lord,” said he, “it-avails-not to anyone to-pursue the lady-chieftain yonder. I-did-not-know a-horse swifter in the realm than that-one, and it-did-not-avail to-me to-pursue her.”
sentences.i: “Lord,” he said, “it is no use for anyone to chase the lady yonder. I knew of no faster horse in the realm than that one, and it was no use to me to chase her.”
sentences.n: y neb 'to anyone'. unbennes is the feminine of unben 'chieftain'; racco 'yonder'. Ny wydwn 'I did not know', imperfect of gwybot, soft after ny. warch is march soft-mutated as the object after the subject i (= uarch): the scribe wrote it with the w-letter for the v-sound. gynt ← kynt 'swifter', comparative of buan. kyuoyth is a spelling of kyuoeth 'realm'. no 'than'. ymi 'to me'.

sentences.t: “Ie,” heb ynteu Pwyll, “y mae yno ryw ystyr hut. Awn parth a'r llys.”
sentences.l: “Yes,” said he-for-his-part Pwyll, “there-is there some meaning of-magic. Let-us-go towards the court.”
sentences.i: “Yes,” said Pwyll, “there is some magic meaning in this. Let us go back to the court.”
sentences.n: y mae yno 'there is there': yno 'there', that is, in this business. ryw ystyr hut: ryw 'some kind of', ystyr 'meaning, purpose', hut 'magic, illusion'. Whether Pwyll means 'some magical purpose' or simply 'some sort of magic' is not certain. Awn 'let us go'. parth a'r llys 'towards the court' (parth a 'towards').

sentences.t: Y'r llys y doethant, a threulau y dyd hwnnw a wnaethant.
sentences.l: To the court they-came, and spending that day they-did.
sentences.i: They came to the court and spent the rest of that day.
sentences.n: Y'r llys y doethant: the adverbial phrase first, then the particle y and the verb (doethant 'they came', preterite plural of dyuot). a threulau 'and spending' ← treulaw (spelt -au here), spirant after a; a wnaethant closes the verbal noun in the plural.

sentences.t: A thrannoeth kyuodi e uynyd a wnaethant, a threulaw hwnnw yny oed amser mynet y uwyta.
sentences.l: And next-day rising up they-did, and spending that until it-was time to-go to eat.
sentences.i: And the next day they got up and passed the time until it was time to go and eat.
sentences.n: A thrannoeth 'and the next day' ← trannoeth, spirant after a. e uynyd = y uynyd 'up'. treulaw hwnnw 'spending that (day)'. yny 'until'. y uwyta 'to eat' ← bwyta, soft after y 'to'.

sentences.t: A gwedy y bwyta kyntaf, “Ie,” heb ynteu Pwyll, “ni a awn yr yniuer y buam doe y penn yr orssed. A thidy,” heb ef wrth vn o'y uakwyueit, “dwg gennyt y march kyntaf a wypych yn y mays.”
sentences.l: And after the first eating, “Yes,” said he-for-his-part Pwyll, “we it-is-that will-go, the company that we-were yesterday, to the top of the mound. And you,” said he to one of his pages, “bring with-you the first horse that you-may-know in the field.”
sentences.i: And after the first sitting at table, “Yes,” said Pwyll, “we will go, the same company we were yesterday, to the top of the mound. And you,” he said to one of his pages, “bring with you the first horse you know of in the field.”
sentences.n: ni a awn 'we will go', the abnormal sentence with a plural verb. y buam doe 'that we were yesterday' (buam, preterite plural of bot). A thidy 'and you' — tidy is the emphatic 'you', spirant after a. o'y uakwyueit 'of his pages' ← makwyueit, plural of makwyf 'page, squire', soft after y 'his'. dwg 'bring', imperative of dwyn; gennyt 'with you'. mays is a spelling of maes 'field'.

sentences.t: A hynny a wnaeth y makwyf.
sentences.l: And that it-was-that did the page.
sentences.i: And the page did so.
sentences.n: A hynny a wnaeth y makwyf: the object first, then a and the verb, and the subject after it — 'that the page did'.

sentences.t: Yr orssed a gyrchyssant, a'r march ganthunt.
sentences.l: The mound they-made-for, and the horse with-them.
sentences.i: They made for the mound, and the horse with them.
sentences.n: a gyrchyssant 'they made for' ← kyrchyssant, a preterite plural in -yssant, soft after a; the object stands first. ganthunt 'with them' (gan conjugated).

sentences.t: Ac val y bydynt yn eiste, wynt a welynt y wreic ar yr vn march, a'r vn wisc amdanei, yn dyuot yr un ford.
sentences.l: And as they-were sitting, they it-was-that saw the woman on the same horse, and the same garment about-her, coming the same way.
sentences.i: And as they sat there, they saw the woman on the same horse, in the same garment, coming the same way.
sentences.n: eiste is eisted with its final -d unwritten; both spellings occur. y wreic 'the woman' ← gwreic, softened after the article because it is feminine. vn wisc ← gwisc, soft after un 'same'. yr un ford: the text prints the article, 'the same road', used as an adverb; it could equally be read y'r 'by the same road', and the manuscript's yr cannot settle which.

sentences.t: “Llyma,” heb y Pwyll, “y uarchoges doe. Bid parawt,” heb ef, “was, e wybot pwy yw hi.”
sentences.l: “Here-is,” said Pwyll, “the horsewoman of-yesterday. Be ready,” said he, “lad, to know who she-is.”
sentences.i: “Here,” said Pwyll, “is yesterday's horsewoman. Be ready, lad,” he said, “to find out who she is.”
sentences.n: Llyma 'here is, behold'. y uarchoges doe 'the horsewoman of yesterday'. Bid is properly the third-person 'let it be'; here it is said to the lad, 'be'. The Red Book has byd, the ordinary second-person imperative, which is what the sense wants. was 'lad' ← gwas, soft in address. e wybot = y wybot 'to know'.

sentences.t: “Arglwyd,” heb ef, “mi a wnaf hynny yn llawen.”
sentences.l: “Lord,” said he, “I it-is-that will-do that gladly.”
sentences.i: “Lord,” he said, “I will do that gladly.”
sentences.n: mi a wnaf 'I will do' — the abnormal sentence. yn llawen 'gladly', the adverbial yn; ll does not mutate after it.

sentences.t: Ar hynny, y uarchoges a doeth gywerbyn ac wynt.
sentences.l: At that, the horsewoman it-was-that came opposite with them.
sentences.i: With that, the horsewoman came level with them.
sentences.n: Ar hynny 'at that, thereupon'. a doeth 'came' (dyuot). gywerbyn ac wynt 'opposite to them' ← kyuerbyn, softened as an adverb; the w here stands for the v-sound.

sentences.t: Sef a oruc y makwyf yna, yskynnu ar y march; a chynn daruot idaw ymgueiraw yn y gyfrwy, neir ry adoed hi heibaw, a chynnwll y rygthunt.
sentences.l: That-is what did the page then: mounting on the horse; and before finishing to-him settling-himself in his saddle, lo she-had-gone past, and a-gap between-them.
sentences.i: The page then mounted the horse; and before he had settled himself in the saddle, she had already gone by, with a gap between them.
sentences.n: Sef a oruc … yskynnu 'that is what he did: mounting' — sef points at the answer. daruot idaw 'finishing to him' = before he had finished (daruot 'be finished, happen', with i/y of the person). ymgueiraw 'make oneself ready'; y gyfrwy ← kyfrwy 'saddle', soft after y 'his'. neir ry adoed: Evans prints neir, clear on the page; it is probably a slip for neur (affirmative neu + 'r), which is what the Red Book has, but the White Book's own reading remains uncertain. ry adoed 'had gone', with perfective ry. kynnwll is a rare word (the Red Book has it too, so it is not this scribe's slip); 'gap, space' is a guess from the context. y rygthunt 'between them'.

sentences.t: Amgen urys gerdet nit oed genthi hi no'r dyd gynt.
sentences.l: Other haste of-pace there-was-not with-her than the day before.
sentences.i: Her pace was no hastier than it had been the day before.
sentences.n: Amgen 'other, different' is the predicate, put first. urys gerdet 'haste of pace' ← brys, kerdet, both soft-mutated: urys after amgen, which softens the noun it governs (as amgen uedwl in the first part). genthi hi 'with her' (gan conjugated, feminine). no'r dyd gynt 'than the day before' (kynt 'earlier').

sentences.t: Ynteu a gymerth rygyng y gan y uarch, ac ef a dybygei yr araued y kerdei y uarch yr ymordiwedei a hi.
sentences.l: He-for-his-part it-was-that took an-amble from his horse, and he it-was-that supposed, for-all the slowness that his horse went, that he-would-overtake her.
sentences.i: He for his part brought his horse to an amble, and thought that, slowly as his horse went, he would catch her up.
sentences.n: rygyng is an easy gait of a horse, an amble; exactly which gait is not certain. y gan y uarch 'from his horse'. a dybygei 'supposed' ← tybygei, soft after a. yr araued y kerdei y uarch: araued (araf 'slow' with the -ed of the equative, 'as slow', used as a noun) 'slowness'; yr … y is probably 'for all the … that' (as yr a ymbilio 'for all that he may beg' in the first part); the phrase is hard and other readings, such as 'at the gentle pace', are possible. yr ymordiwedei 'that he would overtake': yr here is the verbal particle (= yd before a vowel); ymordiwed a 'overtake'.

sentences.t: A hynny ny thygywys idaw.
sentences.l: And that availed-not to-him.
sentences.i: And that did him no good.
sentences.n: ny thygywys 'did not avail' — the preterite in -wys of tygyaw, spirant after ny; the subject hynny stands first (tygyaw 'avail' takes no object).

sentences.t: Ellwg y uarch a oruc wrth auwyneu; nyt oed nes idi yna no chynt bei ar y gam; a phei wyaf y lladei ef y uarch, pellaf uydei hitheu e wrthaw ef; y cherdet hitheu nit oed uwy no chynt.
sentences.l: Loosing his horse he-did by reins; it-was-not nearer to-her then than before, if-it-were at its step; and the most he-would-strike his horse, the farthest she-for-her-part would-be from-him; her pace for-her-part was-not more than before.
sentences.i: He gave his horse its head, but he was no nearer to her then than before, as though it were going at a walk; and the harder he drove his horse, the farther from him she was; yet her own pace was no greater than before.
sentences.n: Ellwg … a oruc 'letting go he did'. wrth auwyneu 'by the reins' (auwyneu, plural of auwyn, modern afwyn 'rein'): probably 'gave it free rein', though the exact force is uncertain. nes 'nearer'; idi 'to her'. no chynt 'than before' ← kynt, spirant after no. bei ar y gam 'if it were at its step' = at a walk: bei, imperfect subjunctive of bot; gam ← cam 'step', soft after y 'its'. The White Book's no chynt bei is awkward; the Red Book has no chyn bei, which reads more smoothly as 'than if it were at a walk'. phei wyaf: pei after a 'and'. wyaf is a scribal slip, one letter short of uwyaf (mwyaf 'most', softened): the scribe writes uwyaf in the parallel sentence above (ffei uwyaf), the Red Book has vwyhaf here, and compare uwy 'more' at the end of this sentence. Kept as Evans prints it; read uwyaf. y cherdet hitheu 'her pace' ← kerdet, spirant after y 'her'. uwy ← mwy 'more'.

sentences.t: Cany welas ef tygyaw idaw e hymlit, ymchwelut a wnaet a dyuot yn yd oet Pwyll.
sentences.l: Since he-saw-not availing to-him her pursuing, returning he-did and coming to where was Pwyll.
sentences.i: Since he saw it was no use to him to chase her, he turned back and came to where Pwyll was.
sentences.n: Cany 'since … not' (can + ny), with welas softened. tygyaw 'availing' is the verbal noun. a wnaet is a scribal slip for a wnaeth (Evans prints it without the h); kept as written. oet is oed, -t for -d.

sentences.t: “Arglwyd,” heb, “nyt oes allu gan y march amgen noc a weleisti.”
sentences.l: “Lord,” said [he], “there-is-not power with the horse other than what you-saw.”
sentences.i: “Lord,” he said, “the horse has no power beyond what you saw.”
sentences.n: Here the White Book leaves a blank after heb; the words nyt oes 'there is not' are supplied from the Red Book, and nothing else is: the tag stands as heb alone, without its ef 'he' (the Red Book reads heb ef nyt oes allu). allu ← gallu 'power', softened after oes. noc a weleisti 'than what you saw': noc is no 'than' before a vowel; weleisti is weleist ti written together.

sentences.t: “Mi a weleis,” heb ynteu, “ny thykya y neb y herlit hi. Ac y rof i a Duw,” heb ef, “yd oed neges idi wrth rei o'r maes hwnn, pei gattei wrthpwythi idi y dywedut. A ni a awn parth a'r llys.”
sentences.l: “I it-is-that saw,” said he-for-his-part, “it-avails-not to anyone to-pursue her. And between me and God,” said he, “there-was an-errand to-her with some of this field, if stubbornness would-allow to-her to-say-it. And we it-is-that will-go towards the court.”
sentences.i: “I saw,” he said, “that it is no use for anyone to chase her. And between me and God,” he said, “she had an errand with someone here in this field, if her stubbornness would let her say it. And we will go back to the court.”
sentences.n: y herlit hi 'to pursue her' — erlit with h- after y 'her'. yd oed neges idi 'there was an errand to her' = she had business. rei o'r maes hwnn 'some of this field' = some of those here. pei gattei 'if (it) would allow', the imperfect subjunctive of gadu. wrthpwythi is a hard word, perhaps found nowhere else, and its meaning is uncertain. The Red Book has wrthpwyll instead (gwrth- 'against' + pwyll 'sense, mind'), which points to something like 'contrariness, perversity'; 'stubbornness' is a guess on that basis. y dywedut 'to say (it)'.

sentences.t: Y'r llys y doethant, a threulaw y nos honno a orugant drwy gerdeu a chyuedach, ual y bu llonyd ganthunt.
sentences.l: To the court they-came, and spending that night they-did through songs and carousing, as it-was content with-them.
sentences.i: They came to the court and spent that night in songs and carousing, as it pleased them.
sentences.n: a orugant 'they did', the plural of a oruc. drwy gerdeu 'through songs' ← kerdeu, plural of kerd, soft after drwy. a chyuedach 'and carousing' ← kyuedach, spirant after a. ual y bu llonyd ganthunt 'as it was content with them' = as they pleased.

sentences.t: A thrannoeth diuyrru y dyd a wnaethant yny oed amser mynet y wwyta.
sentences.l: And next-day passing the day they-did until it-was time to-go to eat.
sentences.i: And the next day they whiled the day away until it was time to go and eat.
sentences.n: diuyrru 'pass (time), divert'. y wwyta: Evans prints wwyta, kept as written; it stands for y uwyta 'to eat' (bwyta, soft after y 'to'; the Red Book has vwyta). It is listed as a slip, though the first w may simply be the w-letter for the v-sound, as in wal and warch above.

sentences.t: A phan daruu udunt y bwyd, Pwyll a dywot, “Mae yr yniuer y buom ni doe ac echtoe ym penn yr orssed?”
sentences.l: And when finished to-them the food, Pwyll it-was-that said, “Where-is the company that we-were yesterday and the-day-before-yesterday on the top of the mound?”
sentences.i: And when they had finished eating, Pwyll said, “Where is the company who were with us yesterday and the day before on top of the mound?”
sentences.n: daruu udunt 'it was finished to them' (daruot; udunt 'to them'). a dywot 'said', preterite. Mae 'where is?' — the question word, not the y mae of 'there is'. buom (= buam) 'we were'. echtoe 'the day before yesterday'. ym penn 'on top of' (yn becomes ym before p).

sentences.t: “Llymma, Arglwyd,” heb wynt.
sentences.l: “Here-it-is, Lord,” said they.
sentences.i: “Here, Lord,” they said.
sentences.n: Llymma is llyma 'here is', with the m doubled.

sentences.t: “Awn,” heb ef, “y'r orssed y eiste. A thitheu,” heb ef wrth was y uarch, “kyfrwya uy march yn da, a dabre ac ef y'r ford, a dwc uy ysparduneu gennyt.”
sentences.l: “Let-us-go,” said he, “to the mound to sit. And you-for-your-part,” said he to the lad of his horse, “saddle my horse well, and come with it to the road, and bring my spurs with-you.”
sentences.i: “Let us go,” he said, “to the mound and sit. And you,” he said to his groom, “saddle my horse well, and come with it to the road, and bring my spurs with you.”
sentences.n: A thitheu 'and you for your part' (titheu, spirant after a). wrth was y uarch 'to the lad of his horse' = his groom; was ← gwas, soft after wrth. kyfrwya 'saddle!' (kyfrwyaw). dabre 'come!', an imperative of dyuot. dwc 'bring!' (dwyn); uy ysparduneu 'my spurs'.

sentences.t: Y gwas a wnaeth hynny.
sentences.l: The lad it-was-that did that.
sentences.i: The lad did so.
sentences.n: Y gwas a wnaeth hynny: subject, a, verb, object — the abnormal sentence.

sentences.t: Dyuot y'r orssed a orugant y eisted.
sentences.l: Coming to the mound they-did, to sit.
sentences.i: They came to the mound to sit.
sentences.n: Dyuot … a orugant: the verbal noun with the plural of a oruc. y eisted 'to sit'.

sentences.t: Ny buant hayach o enkyt yno yny welynt y uarchoges yn dyuot yr vn ford, ac yn un ansawd, ac vn gerdet.
sentences.l: They-were-not hardly of a-while there until they-saw the horsewoman coming the same way, and in the same appearance, and the same pace.
sentences.i: They had hardly been there any while before they saw the horsewoman coming the same way, with the same appearance and at the same pace.
sentences.n: Ny buant 'they were not' (buant, preterite plural of bot). hayach 'hardly, almost'; o enkyt 'of a while'. yny welynt 'until they saw'. yr vn ford again, the same ambiguity (the same road, or by the same road). ansawd 'appearance'; vn gerdet ← kerdet.

sentences.t: “Ha was,” heb y Pwyll, “mi a welaf y uarchoges. Moes uy march.”
sentences.l: “Ha lad,” said Pwyll, “I it-is-that see the horsewoman. Give my horse.”
sentences.i: “Lad,” said Pwyll, “I see the horsewoman. Give me my horse.”
sentences.n: Ha was 'ho, lad!' (gwas, soft in address). mi a welaf 'I see'. Moes 'give (me)!', an old imperative found only in this form.

sentences.t: Yskynnu a oruc Pwyll ar y uarch; ac nyt kynt yd yskynn ef ar y uarch noc yd a hitheu hebdaw ef.
sentences.l: Mounting Pwyll did on his horse; and not sooner does-he-mount on his horse than goes she-for-her-part past-him.
sentences.i: Pwyll mounted his horse; and no sooner was he on it than she had gone past him.
sentences.n: Yskynnu a oruc Pwyll 'mounting Pwyll did'. nyt kynt … noc 'no sooner … than'. yd yskynn 'he mounts' and yd a 'goes' are presents used for vividness, the particle yd before a vowel. hebdaw 'past him' (heb 'without, past', conjugated).

sentences.t: Troi yn y hol a oruc ef, a gadel y uarch drythyll llamsachus y gerdet.
sentences.l: Turning after her he-did, and letting his horse spirited prancing to go.
sentences.i: He turned after her and let his spirited, prancing horse go.
sentences.n: Troi yn y hol 'turning after her' (ol with h- after y 'her'). gadel 'leave, let'. drythyll 'spirited, wanton' ← trythyll, written softened; llamsachus 'prancing, bounding' (llam 'leap'). y gerdet 'to go' ← kerdet, soft after y 'to'.

sentences.t: Ac ef a debygei, ar yr eil neit neu ar y trydyd, y gordiwedei.
sentences.l: And he it-was-that supposed, at the second leap or at the third, that he-would-overtake-her.
sentences.i: And he thought he would overtake her at the second bound or the third.
sentences.n: a debygei 'supposed' ← tybygei. yr eil 'the second', y trydyd 'the third'; neit 'leap'. y gordiwedei 'that he would overtake (her)': y is the verbal particle (one of its five jobs), and gordiwedei the imperfect of gordiwes 'overtake'.

sentences.t: Nyt oed nes hagen idi no chynt.
sentences.l: It-was-not nearer, however, to-her than before.
sentences.i: But he was no nearer to her than before.
sentences.n: nes 'nearer'; hagen 'however'; idi 'to her'; no chynt 'than before'.

sentences.t: Y uarch a gymhellaud o'r kerdet mwyaf a oed ganthaw.
sentences.l: His horse he-urged to the greatest pace that was with-it.
sentences.i: He urged his horse to the greatest speed it had.
sentences.n: a gymhellaud 'urged' ← kymhellawd, the preterite in -awd (here -aud) of kymhell 'urge, compel', soft after a; the object y uarch stands first. o'r kerdet mwyaf 'to (literally 'of') the greatest pace'. ganthaw 'with it'.

sentences.t: A guelet a wnaeth na thygyei idaw y hymlit.
sentences.l: And seeing he-did that it-availed-not to-him her pursuing.
sentences.i: And he saw that it was no use to him to chase her.
sentences.n: A guelet a wnaeth 'and seeing he did'. na thygyei idaw y hymlit, as before.

sentences.t: Yna y dywot Pwyll, “A uorwyn,” heb ef, “yr mwyn y gwr mwyhaf a gery, arho ui.”
sentences.l: Then said Pwyll, “O maiden,” said he, “for-the-sake-of the man that you-love most, wait-for me.”
sentences.i: Then Pwyll said, “Maiden,” he said, “for the sake of the man you love best, wait for me.”
sentences.n: y dywot 'said', with y after Yna. A uorwyn 'O maiden' ← morwyn, soft in address. yr mwyn 'for the sake of'. mwyhaf = mwyaf 'most'. a gery 'that you love' ← kery, present of caru, soft after a. arho 'wait!' (arhos); ui ← mi 'me', softened after the imperative.

sentences.t: “Arhoaf yn llawen,” heb hi, “ac oed llessach y'r march pei ass archut yr meityn.”
sentences.l: “I-will-wait gladly,” said she, “and it-were better for the horse if you-had-asked-it a-while-ago.”
sentences.i: “I will wait gladly,” she said, “and it would have been better for the horse if you had asked it a good while ago.”
sentences.n: Arhoaf 'I will wait' — the answer repeats the verb. oed llessach 'it would be better' (llessach, comparative of lles 'good, benefit'). pei ass archut 'if you had asked it': pei 'if', the infixed 's 'it' (doubled; Evans affarchut), archut the imperfect subjunctive of erchi 'ask'. yr meityn 'for a while (since)' = some time ago.

sentences.t: Sewyll ac arhos a oruc y uorwyn, a gwaret y rann a dylyei uot am y hwyneb o wisc y phenn, ac attal y golwc arnaw, a dechreu ymdidan ac ef.
sentences.l: Stopping and waiting the maiden did, and removing the part that ought to-be about her face of the covering of her head, and fixing her gaze on-him, and beginning to-converse with him.
sentences.i: The maiden stopped and waited, and drew back the part of her head-covering that should have been about her face, and fixed her gaze on him, and began to talk with him.
sentences.n: Sewyll is sefyll 'stand, stop', w for the v-sound. gwaret 'remove'. a dylyei uot 'that ought to be' (dylyei, imperfect of dylyu; uot ← bot). y hwyneb 'her face' (h- after y 'her'); y phenn 'her head' ← penn, spirant after y 'her'. attal y golwc arnaw 'holding her gaze on him'. ymdidan ac ef 'converse with him'.

sentences.t: “Arglwydes,” heb ef, “pan doy di, a pha gerdet yssyd arnat ti?”
sentences.l: “Lady,” said he, “whence come you, and what journey is-there on-you?”
sentences.i: “Lady,” he said, “where do you come from, and what journey are you on?”
sentences.n: Arglwydes 'lady', the feminine of arglwyd. pan doy di 'whence do you come?' — pan is 'from where', doy the present of dyuot. a pha 'and what' (pa, spirant after a). yssyd 'that is', the relative form of bot. arnat ti 'on you'.

sentences.t: “Kerdet wrth uy negesseu,” heb hi, “a da yw gennyf dy welet ti.”
sentences.l: “Going about my errands,” said she, “and good it-is with-me your seeing.”
sentences.i: “Going about my own business,” she said, “and I am glad to see you.”
sentences.n: negesseu 'errands, business', plural of neges. da yw gennyf 'it is good with me' = I am glad. dy welet ti 'your seeing' = to see you: the object as a possessive before the verbal noun, gwelet softened after dy.

sentences.t: “Crassaw wrthyt y gennyf i,” heb ef.
sentences.l: “Welcome to-you from me,” said he.
sentences.i: “You have my welcome,” he said.
sentences.n: Crassaw 'welcome' (modern croeso). wrthyt 'to you'; y gennyf i 'from me'.

sentences.t: Ac yna medylyaw a wnaeth bot yn diuwyn ganthaw pryt a welsei o uorwyn eiroet a gwreic y wrth y ffryt hi.
sentences.l: And then thinking he-did that-was worthless with-him the form that he-had-seen of maiden ever and woman compared-with her form.
sentences.i: And then he thought that the looks of any maiden or woman he had ever seen were worthless beside hers.
sentences.n: medylyaw a wnaeth 'thinking he did'. bot yn diuwyn ganthaw 'being diuwyn in his view': bot carries the 'that … was' clause. diuwyn is di- 'without' + mwyn (softened), 'worthless' or 'unpleasing'; which shade is meant is debated. pryt 'form, looks'. a welsei 'that he had seen', pluperfect in -sei. o uorwyn ← morwyn. y wrth 'compared with', as in the first part. y ffryt hi 'her form' ← pryt, spirant after y 'her', written ff.

sentences.t: “Arglwydes,” heb ef, “a dywedy di ymi dim o'th negesseu?”
sentences.l: “Lady,” said he, “will-you-tell you to-me anything of your errands?”
sentences.i: “Lady,” he said, “will you tell me anything of your business?”
sentences.n: a dywedy di 'will you tell?' — a the question particle, dywedy the present of dywedut. ymi 'to me'; dim 'anything'; o'th 'of your'.

sentences.t: “Dywedaf, y rof a Duw,” heb hi. “Pennaf neges uu ymi keissaw dy welet ti.”
sentences.l: “I-will-tell, between me and God,” said she. “Chief errand that-was to-me seeking your seeing.”
sentences.i: “I will, between me and God,” she said. “My chief errand has been to try to see you.”
sentences.n: Dywedaf 'I will tell' — again the verb answers the question. y rof a Duw, here without its i. Pennaf neges uu 'the chief errand (that) was': uu ← bu, softened. keissaw dy welet ti 'seeking to see you'.

sentences.t: “Llyna,” heb y Pwll, “y neges oreu gennyf i dy dyuot ti idi. Ac a dywedy di ymi pwy wyt?”
sentences.l: “There-is,” said Pwyll, “the errand best with-me your coming to-it. And will-you-tell you to-me who you-are?”
sentences.i: “That,” said Pwyll, “is the errand I would most gladly see you come on. And will you tell me who you are?”
sentences.n: heb y Pwll: the manuscript writes Pwll, a slip for Pwyll; Evans prints it so and it is kept. Llyna 'there is'. y neges oreu gennyf 'the errand best with me' (goreu softened after the feminine neges). dy dyuot ti idi 'your coming to it' — idi is feminine because neges is.

sentences.t: “Dywedaf, Arglwyd,” heb hi. “Riannon uerch Heueyd Hen wyf i, a'm rodi y wr o'm hanwod yd ydys. Ac ny mynneis innheu un gwr, a hynny o'th garyat ti; ac nys mynnaf etwa, onyt ti a'm gwrthyt. Ac e wybot dy attep di am hynny e deuthum i.”
sentences.l: “I-will-tell, Lord,” said she. “Rhiannon daughter of-Hefeydd the-Old am I, and my giving to a-man against-my-will it-is-being-done. And I-did-not-want, I-for-my-part, any man, and that from love-of-you; and I-do-not-want-him yet, unless you reject-me. And to know your answer about that I-came.”
sentences.i: “I will, Lord,” she said. “I am Rhiannon, daughter of Hefeydd the Old, and they are giving me to a husband against my will. But I have wanted no man, and that for love of you; and I want none yet, unless you reject me. And I have come to learn your answer to that.”
sentences.n: Riannon is Rhiannon; Heueyd Hen is Hefeydd the Old; uerch 'daughter' ← merch. a'm rodi 'and my giving' = and (they are) giving me: a 'and' + 'm 'my', which before the verbal noun rodi stands for its object. y wr 'to a man, husband' ← gwr. o'm hanwod 'against my will' ← anuod (modern anfodd), with h- after 'm and w for the v-sound. yd ydys 'it is being (done)', the impersonal present of bot. ny mynneis innheu 'I for my part did not want' (preterite). o'th garyat ti 'from love of you' ← karyat. nys mynnaf 'I do not want him', infixed 's. etwa 'yet'. onyt 'unless'. a'm gwrthyt 'who rejects me' (gwrthot 'refuse'). e deuthum i 'I came', e for the particle y.

sentences.t: “Rof i a Duw,” heb ynteu Pwyll, “llyna uy attep i iti: pei caffwn dewis ar holl wraged a morynnyon y byt, y mae ti a dewisswn.”
sentences.l: “Between me and God,” said he-for-his-part Pwyll, “there-is my answer to-you: if I-were-to-get choice of all the women and maidens of the world, it-is you that I-would-choose.”
sentences.i: “Between me and God,” said Pwyll, “here is my answer to you: if I could have my choice of all the women and maidens in the world, it is you I would choose.”
sentences.n: Rof i a Duw is the formula y rof i a Duw without its y. pei caffwn 'if I were to get', the imperfect subjunctive of caffael. holl wraged 'all the women' ← gwraged, soft after holl; morynnyon 'maidens'. y mae ti a dewisswn 'it is you that I would choose': dewisswn is the imperfect subjunctive of dewis, with the -ss- of the old s-forms.

sentences.t: “Ie,” heb hitheu, “os hynny a uynny, kyn uy rodi y wr arall, gwna oed a mi.”
sentences.l: “Yes,” said she-for-her-part, “if that you-want, before my giving to another man, make an-appointment with me.”
sentences.i: “Yes,” she said, “if that is what you want, then before I am given to another man, make an appointment with me.”
sentences.n: heb hitheu 'said she for her part'. a uynny 'that you want' ← mynny, soft after a. uy rodi 'my giving' = giving me. gwna 'make!' (gwneuthur). oed here (and oet below) is 'appointment, tryst', not the oed 'was'; gwna oed a mi 'make an appointment with me'.

sentences.t: “Goreu yw gennyf i,” heb y Pwyll, “bo kyntaf; ac yn y lle y mynnych ti, gwna yr oet.”
sentences.l: “Best it-is with-me,” said Pwyll, “may-it-be soonest; and in the place that you-may-wish, make the appointment.”
sentences.i: “For my part,” said Pwyll, “soonest is best; and make the appointment in whatever place you wish.”
sentences.n: Goreu yw gennyf 'it is best with me'. bo kyntaf 'may it be soonest' — bo is the present subjunctive of bot. y mynnych 'that you may wish', present subjunctive of mynnu.

sentences.t: “Gwnaf, Arglwyd,” heb hi. “Blwydyn y heno, yn llys Heueyd, mi a baraf bot gwled darparedic yn barawt erbyn dy dyuot.”
sentences.l: “I-will-make, Lord,” said she. “A-year from tonight, in the court of-Hefeydd, I it-is-that will-cause that there-be a-feast prepared ready against your coming.”
sentences.i: “I will, Lord,” she said. “A year from tonight, in Hefeydd's court, I will see to it that a feast is prepared and ready for your coming.”
sentences.n: Gwnaf 'I will make (it)'. Blwydyn y heno 'a year from tonight', the same reckoning as Arawn's appointment in the first part. mi a baraf 'I will cause' ← paraf (peri), soft after a. yn barawt 'ready' ← parawt, soft after the predicative yn. erbyn dy dyuot 'against your coming'.

sentences.t: “Yn llawen,” heb ynteu, “a mi a uydaf yn yr oet hwnnw.”
sentences.l: “Gladly,” said he-for-his-part, “and I it-is-that will-be at that appointment.”
sentences.i: “Gladly,” he said, “and I will be at that appointment.”
sentences.n: mi a uydaf 'I will be' ← bydaf, the future of bot, soft after a. yn yr oet hwnnw 'at that appointment'.

sentences.t: “Arglwyd,” heb hi, “tric yn iach, a choffa gywiraw dy edewit; ac e ymdeith yd af i.”
sentences.l: “Lord,” said she, “stay in health, and remember to-fulfil your promise; and away I-go.”
sentences.i: “Lord,” she said, “farewell, and remember to keep your promise; and now I will be on my way.”
sentences.n: tric yn iach 'stay in health', the farewell (tric, imperative of trigyaw 'stay'). a choffa 'and remember' ← koffa, spirant after a. gywiraw 'make true, fulfil' ← kywiraw, softened. edewit 'promise'. e ymdeith 'away'; yd af i 'I go'.

about: Pwyll is feasting at his court at Arberth, and beside it is a mound with a reputation: any man of rank who sits on it will come away either hurt or having seen a wonder. Pwyll chooses to risk it, and on three days running a woman rides past at an easy pace that no horse can overtake.
